vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: the way you say something, separate from the words you choose
how high or low a voice sounds
the speed at which someone speaks
a flat voice that stays on one note and never rises or falls
to speak quietly and unclearly, so the words blur into each other
the extra weight your voice puts on one word, so the listener knows it matters most
a sound or word such as "um" that you add while you look for the next idea
a short, deliberate silence you place between two ideas

reading.rtitle: Why Correct English Can Still Be Hard to Follow
paras: Portuguese gives almost every syllable the same amount of time. English does not. English runs on strong beats: the content words -- nouns, main verbs, adjectives, numbers, question words and negatives -- get more length, more volume and a higher pitch, while the function words between them (a, the, of, to, in, for, is, was) shrink until they almost disappear. A native listener does not hear every word equally. He hears the strong beats and uses them to find the information. When a speaker gives every word the same weight, nothing is wrong with the English, but the listener has to do all the sorting himself. After about a minute of that work, the room stops listening. Not because the speaker made a mistake, but because listening became tiring.

The second piece is grouping. Fluent English is not a river of words; it is a series of short thought groups, three to seven words each, one idea per group, with a small pause at the end. I led a team of forty engineers / in three countries / for eleven years. The pause goes between the groups and never inside them. Inside each group, one word carries the most emphasis, and it is usually the last content word. Move that emphasis and you change the message without changing a single word: I never said the migration failed can mean four different things, depending on where the weight lands. This is why a pause is not a weakness. A short silence before the number, before the name, before the result is one of the most executive things a voice can do.

The third piece is melody, and it is where careful speakers lose the most. Statements and wh-questions fall at the end; yes-no questions rise. Many Brazilian speakers end a statement on a rising note, and to an American ear a rising statement is a question or a doubt -- so a good, well-prepared answer suddenly sounds unsure. The opposite trap is the flat monotone, which sounds bored or rehearsed. The third trap is speed: under pressure the pace goes up, the pauses disappear, the endings get mumbled and the fillers arrive. Nobody was ever hired for saying more words per minute. Slow down, group the words, land the last one, and let the silence do part of the work.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: English carries meaning in its rhythm and melody: strong content words, short thought groups, one focus word per group, and a falling ending for statements.
The most important thing in an interview is to speak faster and never stop, because a pause makes a speaker sound unsure.
Portuguese and English use the same rhythm, so a Brazilian speaker only needs to correct individual sounds.

gapfill.text: Strong = content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, numbers, negatives). Weak = function words (a, the, of, to, in, is). Group three to seven words, pause between the groups, put the emphasis on the last content word, and let statements fall at the end.

bank.label: Lines that land in an interview
items: I led a team of forty engineers in three countries.
We finished the migration in March.
It was forty engineers, not sixty.
That is a good question. Let me think for a second.
That is not what the data says.
Let me give you the number first, and then the story.
Could you walk me through the numbers?
The short answer is yes. The longer answer takes thirty seconds.

forms.title: Five moves that carry the meaning
cards: "I LED a TEAM of FORTY ENGINEERS." The small words -- a, of, the, to -- get shorter, quieter and lower. That contrast is the rhythm of English.
Three to seven words, one idea
"I led a team of forty engineers / in three countries / for eleven years." A small pause at the end of each group, and never inside one.
"We finished the migration in MARCH." Move it and the message moves: "WE finished it" means another team did not.
"That is what I would do first." The voice goes down at the end. A statement that rises sounds like a doubt to an American listener.
"an old system" sounds like "a-nold system"; "pick it up" sounds like "pi-ki-tup". Native speech joins the words; it does not spell them.

items.situation: A recruiter asks how big the team was. Answer in one thought group and land the number.
tips: I led a team of forty engineers.
The strongest beat goes on FORTY, and the voice falls at the end.

items.situation: You are asked when the migration finished. Answer so that the date is the strongest word in the sentence.
tips: We finished the migration in MARCH.
One group, one focus word, falling ending.

items.situation: The interviewer repeats your number wrongly and says sixty engineers. Correct him without sounding rude.
tips: It was FORTY engineers, not sixty.
Only the corrected word gets the weight -- not the whole sentence.

items.situation: You need two seconds to think in the middle of an answer. Buy the time without a filler.
tips: That is a good question. -- and then simply stop.
Silence costs nothing. Um costs credibility.

items.situation: Give your role and your years of experience in two thought groups.
tips: I am a technology executive / with more than forty years in the industry.
A small pause between the groups, and the second one falls.

items: Round 1 -- Guided
Say three facts about your career, one thought group each: your role, the size of your team, the number of years. Pause between the groups and let every ending fall.
Round 2 -- Move the focus
Say "We finished the migration in March" four times, each time with the emphasis on a different word, and say in English what each version means.
Round 3 -- Under pressure
Answer "Tell me about your biggest project" in sixty seconds. Every time you want to say um, pause instead.
Curveball
Answer the same question in thirty seconds, and make sure the last word of every sentence falls.

answerkey.title: Reveal the marked-up model answer
list: Model, marked up: "I am a technology executive / with more than FORTY YEARS in the industry. // I spent most of that time at IBM, / where I led a team of forty ENGINEERS / in three COUNTRIES. // The project I am proudest of / is the platform migration we finished in MARCH. // It was late twice, / and it did not FAIL. // Today I work on AI SAFETY, / and that is where I want the next ten years to go."
The single slash is a short pause between thought groups. The double slash is a full stop, where the voice falls all the way down.
The capital letters are the focus words -- the last content word of each group, unless you are correcting something.
Note what is NOT strong: am, a, with, than, in, the, of, and, that, is. Those words run fast and low, and that speed is what creates the rhythm.
The negative is always strong: it did not FAIL.
Rule of thumb for the room: no group longer than seven words, no pause inside a group, and every statement falling at the end.
answerkey.note: Read the model out loud twice: once exactly as marked, and once at your normal speed. The second reading is the one to record.

listenings.text: I work with senior people whose English is already good, and almost all of them arrive with the same question. They ask me how to lose the accent. That is not the question. Nobody in an American meeting is scoring your vowels. What they are doing, without knowing it, is following your strong beats. English gives length and height to the words that carry information, and it runs fast and low over everything else, so the listener can find the meaning without effort. When every word arrives with the same weight, nothing is wrong. The grammar is fine, the vocabulary is often better than mine. But the listener now has to sort the sentence himself, and sorting is work. After about a minute of that work, attention goes. People will tell you afterwards that you were hard to follow, and you will think they meant your pronunciation. They did not. They meant they got tired. So here is the first thing I ask for. Break the answer into short groups, three to seven words, and put a real silence at the end of each one. And the second thing. When you need a moment, close your mouth and take it. Do not say um. Silence costs you nothing. A filler costs you credibility, every single time.

Quick note before I forget the day. Two candidates, and the difference had nothing to do with their level of English. The first one, technically, was excellent. Her grammar was close to perfect, better than most native speakers on that panel. But she spoke in one long line, at one speed, with no landing anywhere, and by the fifteen minute mark I had stopped hearing individual sentences. When I read my own notes afterwards I could not tell you what her biggest project was. That is not a language problem. That is a delivery problem, and it cost her the room. The second candidate had a much heavier accent and made two grammar mistakes I noticed. She also did something that I want every candidate to do. I asked her the hardest question of the day, about a program that went badly, and instead of filling the air she stopped. She stayed silent for maybe two seconds, and the whole panel leaned in. Then she gave us three short sentences, each one ending on a full stop you could hear. Everybody in that room remembers her answer. So when you talk to the next group, tell them this from me. Slow down and use the silence. Nobody in the history of this company has ever been rejected for pausing.

extra_audio.text: First I break the answer into short groups of three to seven words. Then I choose the one word in each group that carries the meaning. I put a small pause at the end of every group. I let my voice fall at the end of every statement. And when I need a second, I pause instead of saying um.
